entries.knowledge: The current diff appended an explicit temperature-conditioning clause to the general non-desklamp acquisition step: for tasks requiring heating or cooling with an appliance (microwave or fridge), bring the target and appliance together and perform the explicit 'heat X with microwave' / 'cool X with fridge' action directly on the held target as soon as it is admissible, even before opening the appliance; open the appliance only if the action is otherwise unavailable; a single heat/cool action is sufficient; do not impose extra close/open cycles on the door or repeatedly move the target into and out of the appliance; for cooling, cool the held object at the fridge without door toggling; then carry the conditioned target straight to the destination. This mirrors the temperature-transformation guidance recorded from the earlier edits (S1_R03, S1_R04), but in this experiment the Parent skill lacked any such clause, so the clause's response could be examined directly. The clearest response occurred in a heat-tomato-to-fridge pair: the Parent took the tomato, opened the microwave, moved the tomato in, then ran many close/open/examine cycles, eventually took the tomato back out and only heated it late (P4:36) before placing it, finishing in 39 steps; the Candidate went to the still-closed microwave and heated the held tomato immediately (Q4:6), then carried it to the fridge and placed it, finishing in 8 steps. A milder version recurred in another heat-tomato-to-fridge pair where the Parent opened the microwave before heating while the Candidate heated the held tomato at the closed microwave (7 steps), and in the cool-plate pair where the Candidate cooled the held plate at the closed fridge without opening it (Q1:7) while the Parent opened the fridge first (P1:5, P1:6); both succeeded. Both sides also cooled while holding when the fridge was already open (P2:15, Q2:7), so the clause is not the only way the action is performed. The evidence supports that, conditional on the exact target having been acquired, the clause is associated with markedly less appliance manipulation and fewer steps, and the Parent's heavy door-toggling shows the failure mode it targets. Limitations: the clause had no opportunity when the target could not be found — in a heat-apple pair the target was absent, no temperature action was attempted, and both Parent and Candidate cycled and hit the step limit; the extreme Parent toggling is a single run; and the clause was edited together with a search-step refinement, so in pairs where search paths also differ (e.g. the 39-step vs 8-step pair) the step-count difference cannot be attributed to the temperature clause alone.

The general non-desklamp search step — which already carried the earlier single-pass family sweep (open each closed container once upon reaching it, and after one family yields nothing move to a different uninspected family before revisiting earlier locations) — was further refined to add three clauses: (i) treat each individual closed container (cabinet, drawer, fridge, microwave, safe, etc.) and each open surface as a separate candidate, and do not treat a container family as finished merely because one or two of its members were empty; (ii) after arriving at an already-open empty receptacle, or one whose visible contents match a location already inspected, do not open, re-examine, or linger there but leave immediately for a not-yet-inspected receptacle; and (iii) if the same small set of locations keeps reappearing in recent observations without yielding the target, stop revisiting them and continue to new candidates while the step budget allows. Observed responses were mixed. In a two-book-to-desk pair the Parent cycled desk1/shelf1/shelf2/drawer1/drawer2 and hit the step limit without ever visiting the bed; the Candidate also cycled for many steps but eventually reached bed1 (Q6:33), found both books there, and completed the two placements (Q6:34–Q6:40), succeeding in 40 steps. In a cool-bread pair the Parent cycled among fridge/countertop1/cabinet1/toaster before finding the bread (18 steps), whereas the Candidate skipped those empty locations and went fridge→countertop1→countertop2 (Q2:4), taking the bread and finishing in 10 steps. In a two-creditcard pair both succeeded, with the Candidate going straight to the desk (9 steps) versus the Parent's drawer sweep (24 steps), but this may reflect location ordering rather than the clause. The clause did not overcome an absent target: in a heat-apple pair neither side found an apple, both cycled among the fridge, countertops and cabinets, and both hit the step limit. The 'leave an already-open empty receptacle immediately' and anti-cycling clauses were also not reliably followed: the Candidate frequently revisited already-open empty drawers/shelves (Q6 spent many steps cycling before reaching the bed; Q3 cycled for the full budget). Limitations: one run per task, container contents and target locations vary across instances, the one clear rescue required the target to be present in a still-uninspected location, and the new clauses were edited together with the temperature clause on a pre-existing sweep, so task-level outcomes cannot be attributed to the new search clauses alone.
